title: Checking Units
text:
ANSYS Mechanical Automation: Checking Units
One of the most tedious parts of automation in ANSYS is unit inconsistency. Rather than having to double check everything, I usually just use the below script as a mechanical snippet (the code is run every solve).
In a case where the same script is used across multiple projects, consider placing a unit checker at the top of your code.
# Accepted units: "m", "cm", "mm", or "um"
unit = "mm"

unitSystems = {
    "m": MechanicalUnitSystem.StandardMKS,
    "cm": MechanicalUnitSystem.StandardCGS,
    "mm": MechanicalUnitSystem.StandardNMM,
    "um": MechanicalUnitSystem.StandardUMKS
}

ExtAPI.Application.ActiveUnitSystem = unitSystems[unit]

print("Active unit system:", unit)

title: Creating Coordinate Systems From CSV
text:
ANSYS Mechanical Automation: Coordinate Systems From CSV
Often times clients will provide CSV files with information; in this case, I was given coordinate a table with coordinate systems’ locations and their names.
To accomplish this, I went through by row (ignoring the first), and edited the coordinate system object per iteration:
import csv

cs = Model.CoordinateSystems

file = '<PATH>'

with open(file, 'r') as csvF:
    reader = csv.reader(csvF)
    next(reader)
    
    for x in reader:
        newCS = cs.AddCoordinateSystem()
        newCS.Name = r"""""" + x[0] 
        newCS.OriginDefineBy = CoordinateSystemAlignmentType.Fixed
        
        newCS.OriginX = Quantity(float(x[1]), "m")
        newCS.OriginY = Quantity(float(x[2]), "m")
        newCS.OriginZ = Quantity(float(x[3]), "m")

title: Creating RPs From NSs
text:
ANSYS Mechanical Automation - Remote Point Pairs from Named Selections
For this project, I needed to represent a six-degree-of-freedom spring between tracks (stationary) and rollers (dynamic). This approach used pairs of remote points that had translational/rotational constraints and whose initial position was determined by the average between the centroids.
If more pairs were required, it would definetly be worthwhile to replace the hardcoded filtering and function sequence with a dictionary that could be looped through.
def avgOfCentroids(nsList):
    pts = []
    x = y = z = 0

    for ns in nsList:
        for id in ns.Location.Ids:
            pts.append(ExtAPI.DataModel.GeoData.GeoEntityById(id).Centroid)

    for p in pts:
        x += p[0]
        y += p[1]
        z += p[2]
    return x/len(pts), y/len(pts), z/len(pts)

def createRPs(nsList):
    coords = avgOfCentroids(nsList)
    for ns in nsList:
        c = Model.RemotePoints.AddRemotePoint()
        c.Name = ns.Name
        c.XCoordinate = Quantity(coords[0], "m")
        c.YCoordinate = Quantity(coords[1], "m")
        c.ZCoordinate = Quantity(coords[2], "m")
        c.PilotNodeAPDLName = ns.Name

        c.ScopingMethod = GeometryDefineByType.Component
        c.Location = ns

Ns = DataModel.GetObjectsByName("Named Selections")[0].Children

xRollers = [x for x in Ns if "xRoller" in x.Name]
zRollers = [x for x in Ns if "zRoller" in x.Name]
xSensors = [x for x in Ns if "xSensor" in x.Name]
zSensors = [x for x in Ns if "zSensor" in x.Name]
zSprings = [x for x in Ns if "ySpring" in x.Name]
thtaRollers = [x for x in Ns if "thRoller" in x.Name]

createRPs(xRollers)
createRPs(zRollers)
createRPs(xSensors)
createRPs(zSensors)
createRPs(zSprings)
createRPs(thtaRollers)

title: Automating 6DOF Bushing Contacts
text:
ANSYS Mechanical Automation: Creating 6DOF Bushing Contacts



Result of running script


When solving a mechanical model, points of contact can become extremely computationally demanding, requiring a heavily refined mesh around the contact region to determine local behavior. For some analyses, however, we do not require an accurate local representation and care more about the overall stiffness between two components.
In this case, we can simplify the expensive contact region with a 6 degree-of-freedom bushing joint, allowing us to represent the connection without the need for an extremely fine mesh.
The challenge to this approach is placing the bushing correctly. With the automation script I wrote below, all of the geometry difficulties are taken care of. The user must select 2 bodies (sphere + cylinder) and the script places a bushing contact lined up along the vector from the center of the sphere and cylinder.
(See end for notes about the code)
import numpy as np

_start_vars = set(dir())

def checkJ(cons):
    for x in cons:
        if "Joint" in str(x.ConnectionType):
            return x
    return None
    
def det3(M):
    return M[0][0]*(M[1][1]*M[2][2] - M[1][2]*M[2][1]) - M[0][1]*(M[1][0]*M[2][2] - M[1][2]*M[2][0]) + M[0][2]*(M[1][0]*M[2][1] - M[1][1]*M[2][0])

globals()['det3'] = det3

def solve_3x3(A, B):
    D = det3(A)
    Ax = [
        [B[0], A[0][1], A[0][2]],
        [B[1], A[1][1], A[1][2]],
        [B[2], A[2][1], A[2][2]]
    ]

    Ay = [
        [A[0][0], B[0], A[0][2]],
        [A[1][0], B[1], A[1][2]],
        [A[2][0], B[2], A[2][2]]
    ]

    Az = [
        [A[0][0], A[0][1], B[0]],
        [A[1][0], A[1][1], B[1]],
        [A[2][0], A[2][1], B[2]]
    ]

    return [det3(Ax)/D, det3(Ay)/D, det3(Az)/D]

globals()['solve_3x3'] = solve_3x3
    
def sphere_center(p1, p2, p3, p4):
    x1, y1, z1 = p1
    A = []
    B = []
    for x, y, z in [p2, p3, p4]:
        A.append([2*(x - x1), 2*(y - y1), 2*(z - z1)])
        B.append(x*x + y*y + z*z - x1*x1 - y1*y1 - z1*z1)

    return solve_3x3(A, B)



globals()['sphere_center'] = sphere_center

selected = list(ExtAPI.SelectionManager.CurrentSelection)

if "Sphere" in str(ExtAPI.DataModel.GeoData.GeoEntityById(selected[0]).SurfaceType):
    cylID = selected[1]
    sphereID = selected[0]
else:
    cylID = selected[0]
    sphereID = selected[1]

sph = ExtAPI.DataModel.GeoData.GeoEntityById(sphereID)
cyl = ExtAPI.DataModel.GeoData.GeoEntityById(cylID)

sphere = sph.Points
norms = cyl.Normals

norms = np.array(norms).reshape(-1, 3)
sphere = np.array(sphere).reshape(-1, 3)

p1 = norms[2]
p2 = norms[7]
p3 = norms[14]

A = np.vstack((p1, p2, p3))

eigenvalues, Vectors = np.linalg.eig(A)
D = np.diag(eigenvalues)

U, s, Vt = np.linalg.svd(norms, full_matrices=True)
S = np.zeros((norms.shape[0], norms.shape[1]))
np.fill_diagonal(S, s)

dirCyl = np.array(Vt[2])

cs = Model.CoordinateSystems
cs1 = cs.AddCoordinateSystem()

selection = ExtAPI.SelectionManager.CreateSelectionInfo(SelectionTypeEnum.GeometryEntities)
selection.Ids = [cylID]

cs1.OriginLocation = selection

sphereCenter = np.array(sphere_center(sphere[0], sphere[10], sphere[20], sphere[30]))

cs1.PrimaryAxis = CoordinateSystemAxisType.PositiveZAxis
cs1.PrimaryAxisDirection = Vector3D(dirCyl[0], dirCyl[1], dirCyl[2])

pointOnCylAxis = np.array([
    float(str(cs1.OriginX).split(" ")[0]),
    float(str(cs1.OriginY).split(" ")[0]),
    float(str(cs1.OriginZ).split(" ")[0])
])

OP = np.array(pointOnCylAxis-sphereCenter)

AtoC = np.cross(np.cross(OP, dirCyl), dirCyl)

AtoC = AtoC / np.linalg.norm(AtoC)

actual_point = sphereCenter + sph.Radius*AtoC

cs1.OriginX = Quantity(str(actual_point[0]) + " [m]")
cs1.OriginY = Quantity(str(actual_point[1]) + " [m]")
cs1.OriginZ = Quantity(str(actual_point[2]) + " [m]")

cs1.PrimaryAxis = CoordinateSystemAxisType.PositiveZAxis
cs1.PrimaryAxisDirection = Vector3D(AtoC)

cs1.SecondaryAxis = CoordinateSystemAxisType.PositiveXAxis
cs1.SecondaryAxisDirection = Vector3D(dirCyl)

cons = Model.Connections.Children

group = checkJ(cons)

if checkJ(cons) is None:
    group = Model.Connections.AddConnectionGroup()

group.ConnectionType = AutoDetectionType.Joint

joint = group.AddJoint()
joint.Type = JointType.Bushing

rp1 = Model.RemotePoints.AddRemotePoint()
rp2 = Model.RemotePoints.AddRemotePoint()

selection = ExtAPI.SelectionManager.CreateSelectionInfo(SelectionTypeEnum.GeometryEntities)
selection.Ids = [cylID]

rp1.Location = selection

selection = ExtAPI.SelectionManager.CreateSelectionInfo(SelectionTypeEnum.GeometryEntities)
selection.Ids = [sphereID]

rp2.Location = selection

joint.ReferenceLocation = rp1
joint.MobileLocation = rp2

rp1.CoordinateSystem = cs2
rp2.CoordinateSystem = cs2
To see the actual math behind this: (INSERT HERE)
When it came to finding the center of the sphere, I recycled it from one of my older scripts before found out how to use CPython (numpy) in ansys mechanical so there are multiple technically not needed functions above that do smaller scale matrix operations.
Because CPython is still technically in beta, there are many weird bugs when it comes to compiling these scripts. In this code specifically, I had to force various functions to be considered global so I could access them at all using globals()['sphere_center'] = sphere_center.
If this code were to be used for a large amount of connections, I would recommend writing a function which sorts your selections into pairs based on centroid proximity and looping through these pairs with the above code.

title: An Object-Oriented Python Wrapper for FEMM
An Object-Oriented Python Wrapper for FEMM
text:
FEMM must be installed before Python can control it. The Python interface can then be installed with:
python -m pip install pyfemm
The wrapper follows camelCase for its own variables and methods. Calls such as mi_addblocklabel() retain pyFEMM’s original names because they are part of the external API.
FemmModel always opens a magnetics document (newdocument(0)). Its default frequency of 0 defines a magnetostatic problem. For a planar model, depth is the physical into-the-page depth; for an axisymmetric model, FEMM expects that value to be 0, so the wrapper sets it automatically. minAngle is a separate mesh-quality constraint—30 degrees is FEMM’s usual value. In an axisymmetric model, the coordinates represent the r-z plane and radial coordinates should not be negative.

title: An Object-Oriented Python Wrapper for FEMM
text:
import femm


class FemmModel:
    """A small object-oriented interface for FEMM magnetics problems."""

    def __init__(
        self,
        axisymmetric=False,
        lengthUnit="millimeters",
        frequency=0,
        precision=1e-8,
        depth=30,
        minAngle=30,
    ):
        self.axisymmetric = axisymmetric
        self.blocks = []
        self.materials = {}
        self.circuits = {}

        femm.openfemm()
        femm.newdocument(0)

        problemType = "axi" if axisymmetric else "planar"
        problemDepth = 0 if axisymmetric else depth

        femm.mi_probdef(
            frequency,
            lengthUnit,
            problemType,
            precision,
            problemDepth,
            minAngle,
        )

    def addBlock(
        self,
        material,
        shape,
        coords,
        direction=0,
        labelPoint=None,
        meshSize=None,
        name=None,
        group=0,
    ):
        block = Block(
            material=material,
            shape=shape,
            coords=coords,
            direction=direction,
            labelPoint=labelPoint,
            meshSize=meshSize,
            name=name,
            group=group,
        )
        self.blocks.append(block)
        return block

    def addCoil(
        self,
        material,
        coords,
        current,
        turns,
        circuitName="coil",
        series=True,
        labelPoint=None,
        meshSize=None,
        name=None,
        group=0,
    ):
        circuitType = 1 if series else 0

        if circuitName not in self.circuits:
            femm.mi_addcircprop(circuitName, current, circuitType)
            self.circuits[circuitName] = {
                "current": current,
                "series": series,
            }
        else:
            circuit = self.circuits[circuitName]
            if circuit["current"] != current or circuit["series"] != series:
                raise ValueError(
                    f"Circuit '{circuitName}' already has different settings"
                )

        coil = Block(
            material=material,
            shape="rectangle",
            coords=coords,
            labelPoint=labelPoint,
            meshSize=meshSize,
            name=name or circuitName,
            group=group,
            circuitName=circuitName,
            turns=turns,
        )
        self.blocks.append(coil)
        return coil

    def loadMaterial(self, materialName):
        femm.mi_getmaterial(materialName)
        material = Material(materialName)
        self.materials[materialName] = material
        return material

    def createMaterial(
        self,
        materialName,
        relativePermeabilityX=1,
        relativePermeabilityY=1,
        coercivity=0,
        currentDensity=0,
        conductivity=0,
        laminationThickness=0,
        hysteresisAngleMax=0,
        laminationFill=1,
        laminationType=0,
        hysteresisAngleX=0,
        hysteresisAngleY=0,
        strandCount=0,
        wireDiameter=0,
    ):
        femm.mi_addmaterial(
            materialName,
            relativePermeabilityX,
            relativePermeabilityY,
            coercivity,
            currentDensity,
            conductivity,
            laminationThickness,
            hysteresisAngleMax,
            laminationFill,
            laminationType,
            hysteresisAngleX,
            hysteresisAngleY,
            strandCount,
            wireDiameter,
        )

        material = Material(materialName)
        self.materials[materialName] = material
        return material

    def setCircuitCurrent(self, circuitName, current):
        if circuitName not in self.circuits:
            raise ValueError(f"Unknown circuit '{circuitName}'")

        femm.mi_setcurrent(circuitName, current)
        self.circuits[circuitName]["current"] = current

    def drawAll(self):
        for block in self.blocks:
            block.draw()

    def solve(self, filePath, minimize=True):
        femm.mi_saveas(str(filePath))
        femm.mi_analyze(1 if minimize else 0)
        femm.mi_loadsolution()

    def getEnergyTable(self):
        energyTable = []

        for block in self.blocks:
            energy, coEnergy = block.getEnergy()
            energyTable.append(
                {
                    "block": block.name,
                    "energy": energy,
                    "coEnergy": coEnergy,
                }
            )

        return energyTable

    def getForceOnBlocks(self, blockList):
        if not blockList:
            raise ValueError("blockList must contain at least one block")

        femm.mo_clearblock()
        for block in blockList:
            block.select()

        forceX = femm.mo_blockintegral(18)
        forceY = femm.mo_blockintegral(19)
        femm.mo_clearblock()
        return forceX, forceY

    def close(self):
        femm.closefemm()


class Block:
    """A closed region, its block label, and its FEMM properties."""

    validShapes = {
        "polygon",
        "circle",
        "rectangle",
        "rectangleCorners",
    }

    def __init__(
        self,
        material,
        shape,
        coords,
        direction=0,
        labelPoint=None,
        meshSize=None,
        name=None,
        group=0,
        circuitName="<None>",
        turns=0,
    ):
        if shape not in self.validShapes:
            validShapeList = ", ".join(sorted(self.validShapes))
            raise ValueError(f"shape must be one of: {validShapeList}")

        self.material = str(material)
        self.shape = shape
        self.coords = list(coords)
        self.direction = direction
        self.labelPoint = tuple(labelPoint) if labelPoint is not None else None
        self.meshSize = 0 if meshSize is None else meshSize
        self.autoMesh = 1 if meshSize is None else 0
        self.name = name or f"{self.material} {self.shape}"
        self.group = group
        self.circuitName = circuitName
        self.turns = turns
        self.isDrawn = False

    def draw(self):
        if self.isDrawn:
            return

        shapeDrawers = {
            "polygon": self._drawPolygon,
            "circle": self._drawCircle,
            "rectangle": self._drawRectangle,
            "rectangleCorners": self._drawRectangleCorners,
        }
        automaticLabelPoint = shapeDrawers[self.shape]()
        labelX, labelY = self.labelPoint or automaticLabelPoint

        femm.mi_addblocklabel(labelX, labelY)
        femm.mi_selectlabel(labelX, labelY)
        femm.mi_setblockprop(
            self.material,
            self.autoMesh,
            self.meshSize,
            self.circuitName,
            self.direction,
            self.group,
            self.turns,
        )
        femm.mi_clearselected()

        self.labelPoint = (labelX, labelY)
        self.isDrawn = True

    def _drawPolygon(self):
        if len(self.coords) < 6 or len(self.coords) % 2 != 0:
            raise ValueError("A polygon needs at least three x-y coordinate pairs")

        pointList = list(zip(self.coords[::2], self.coords[1::2]))

        for pointIndex, startPoint in enumerate(pointList):
            endPoint = pointList[(pointIndex + 1) % len(pointList)]
            femm.mi_drawline(
                startPoint[0],
                startPoint[1],
                endPoint[0],
                endPoint[1],
            )

        xValues = [point[0] for point in pointList]
        yValues = [point[1] for point in pointList]
        return (
            (min(xValues) + max(xValues)) / 2,
            (min(yValues) + max(yValues)) / 2,
        )

    def _drawCircle(self):
        self._requireCoordinateCount(3)
        centerX, centerY, radius = self.coords

        if radius <= 0:
            raise ValueError("Circle radius must be positive")

        femm.mi_drawarc(
            centerX,
            centerY + radius,
            centerX,
            centerY - radius,
            180,
            30,
        )
        femm.mi_drawarc(
            centerX,
            centerY - radius,
            centerX,
            centerY + radius,
            180,
            30,
        )
        return centerX, centerY

    def _drawRectangle(self):
        self._requireCoordinateCount(4)
        centerX, centerY, width, height = self.coords

        if width <= 0 or height <= 0:
            raise ValueError("Rectangle width and height must be positive")

        femm.mi_drawrectangle(
            centerX - width / 2,
            centerY - height / 2,
            centerX + width / 2,
            centerY + height / 2,
        )
        return centerX, centerY

    def _drawRectangleCorners(self):
        self._requireCoordinateCount(4)
        firstX, firstY, secondX, secondY = self.coords
        minX, maxX = sorted((firstX, secondX))
        minY, maxY = sorted((firstY, secondY))

        if minX == maxX or minY == maxY:
            raise ValueError("Rectangle corners must define a nonzero area")

        femm.mi_drawrectangle(minX, minY, maxX, maxY)
        return (minX + maxX) / 2, (minY + maxY) / 2

    def _requireCoordinateCount(self, expectedCount):
        if len(self.coords) != expectedCount:
            raise ValueError(
                f"{self.shape} requires {expectedCount} coordinate values"
            )

    def select(self):
        if not self.isDrawn:
            raise RuntimeError(f"Block '{self.name}' has not been drawn")

        femm.mo_selectblock(*self.labelPoint)

    def getForce(self):
        femm.mo_clearblock()
        self.select()
        forceX = femm.mo_blockintegral(18)
        forceY = femm.mo_blockintegral(19)
        femm.mo_clearblock()
        return forceX, forceY

    def getEnergy(self):
        femm.mo_clearblock()
        self.select()
        energy = femm.mo_blockintegral(2)
        coEnergy = femm.mo_blockintegral(17)
        femm.mo_clearblock()
        return energy, coEnergy


class Material:
    """A reference to a material in the active FEMM document."""

    def __init__(self, materialName):
        self.materialName = materialName

    def addBhPoints(self, bhPoints):
        for fluxDensity, fieldIntensity in bhPoints:
            femm.mi_addbhpoint(
                self.materialName,
                fluxDensity,
                fieldIntensity,
            )
        return self

    def clearBhPoints(self):
        femm.mi_clearbhpoints(self.materialName)
        return self

    def __str__(self):
        return self.materialName

title: An Object-Oriented Python Wrapper for FEMM
text:
Each block takes a material, a shape, and a flat coordinate list. The supported shapes are:



Shape
Coordinate format




polygon
[x1, y1, x2, y2, ...]


circle
[centerX, centerY, radius]


rectangle
[centerX, centerY, width, height]


rectangleCorners
[x1, y1, x2, y2]



The wrapper places a block label at the geometric center by default. That is convenient for simple, isolated regions. For a concave polygon, a hollow region, or nested geometry, the center may not lie in the intended material region. In those cases, pass a known interior point explicitly with labelPoint=[x, y].
meshSize=None lets FEMM choose the mesh density. Passing a number disables automatic meshing for that block and uses the supplied local element-size constraint.
Multiple coil blocks can share a circuitName as long as they use the same current and connection type. Signed values for turns can represent opposite winding directions. The force methods use FEMM’s weighted stress-tensor block integrals, so their usual region-selection and surrounding-air requirements still apply.

title: An Object-Oriented Python Wrapper for FEMM
text:
The example below defines a planar problem, loads standard materials, adds a custom nonlinear material, creates geometry, solves it, and reads the core energy. The B-H values are illustrative placeholders rather than measured material data.
model = FemmModel(
    axisymmetric=False,
    lengthUnit="millimeters",
    depth=30,
)

air = model.loadMaterial("Air")
copper = model.loadMaterial("Copper")

coreMaterial = model.createMaterial("Measured core")
coreMaterial.addBhPoints(
    [
        (0.00, 0),
        (0.50, 80),
        (1.00, 180),
        (1.40, 600),
        (1.60, 2500),
    ]
)

model.addBlock(
    material=air,
    shape="rectangleCorners",
    coords=[-80, -60, 80, 60],
    labelPoint=[70, 50],
    name="surrounding air",
)

coreBlock = model.addBlock(
    material=coreMaterial,
    shape="rectangle",
    coords=[0, 0, 40, 10],
    meshSize=0.5,
    name="steel core",
)

model.addCoil(
    material=copper,
    coords=[0, 20, 30, 10],
    current=1.0,
    turns=200,
    circuitName="driveCoil",
)

model.drawAll()

# Add the boundary condition required by the physical model here.
# Direct pyFEMM calls remain available for features outside the wrapper.

model.solve(r"C:\femm\models\coreStudy.fem")

energy, coEnergy = coreBlock.getEnergy()
print(f"Core energy: {energy}")
print(f"Core co-energy: {coEnergy}")

model.close()
This is intentionally not a complete physical model: the correct outer boundary, excitation, material data, and mesh-convergence study depend on the problem being solved. The wrapper handles repetitive model construction; it does not hide those engineering decisions.

title: An Object-Oriented Python Wrapper for FEMM
text:
The main benefit appears when the same model must be solved repeatedly. For example, a current sweep can update the circuit without reconstructing the geometry:
currentValues = [-2, -1, 0, 1, 2]
fieldResults = []

for current in currentValues:
    model.setCircuitCurrent("driveCoil", current)
    model.solve(r"C:\femm\models\currentSweep.fem")

    fluxDensity = femm.mo_getb(0, 0)
    fieldIntensity = femm.mo_geth(0, 0)

    fieldResults.append(
        {
            "current": current,
            "fluxDensity": fluxDensity,
            "fieldIntensity": fieldIntensity,
        }
    )
That repeatability was the reason for writing the wrapper. In the hysteresis study, the geometry and result extraction stayed fixed while excitation and material inputs changed between solves.
One important distinction: an automated current sweep is not, by itself, a hysteresis model. The physical meaning of the result still depends on the chosen FEMM material representation, B-H data, solver settings, and sweep procedure. The wrapper only makes that procedure easier to express and reproduce.

title: An Object-Oriented Python Wrapper for FEMM
text:
Block.draw()
Draws the block geometry in FEMM and assigns its material and mesh properties.
block.draw()
The geometry created depends on block.shape.

coordlist
Coordinates are supplied as sequential XY pairs:
[x1, y1, x2, y2, x3, y3, ...]
Lines are drawn between each pair of points to form a closed shape.


circle
Coordinates use:
[centerX, centerY, radius]
The circle is created using two 180° arcs.


rectangle
Coordinates use:
[centerX, centerY, width, height]
The rectangle is constructed around the specified center.


rectangle corners
Coordinates use:
[x1, y1, x2, y2]
The two coordinate pairs define opposite corners of the rectangle.
After creating the geometry, draw() adds a FEMM block label and assigns the block’s material, mesh size, and magnetization direction.

title: An Object-Oriented Python Wrapper for FEMM
text:
from femmModel import Model

# Create an axisymmetric FEMM model
model = Model(radius=50, symetric=True)

# Load materials from FEMM's material library
air = model.loadMaterial("Air")
copper = model.loadMaterial("Copper")
iron = model.loadMaterial("Pure Iron")

# Create an air region
airBlock = model.addBlock(
    material=air,
    shape="rectangle",
    coords=[0, 0, 100, 100]
)

# Create an iron core
core = model.addBlock(
    material=iron,
    shape="rectangle",
    coords=[20, 0, 20, 50]
)

# Create a circular iron block
disk = model.addBlock(
    material=iron,
    shape="circle",
    coords=[40, 0, 10]
)

# Draw every block in the model
model.drawAll()

# Solve the FEMM model
model.solve()

# Get the force acting on the iron blocks
fx, fy = model.getForceOnBlocks([core, disk])

print("Force X:", fx)
print("Force Y:", fy)

# Get energy and co-energy for each block
energyTable = model.getEnergyTable()

print("\nEnergy Table:")
print(energyTable)
